texts.value: Multifunctional copper-sensing protein that operates both as a cytosolic copper chaperone and as a copper-dependent transcription factor. Essential for maintaining cellular copper homeostasis and linking copper distribution to redox balance, signal transduction, and gene regulation. In the cytosol, transfers copper to the copper-transporting ATPase ATP7A at the trans-Golgi network, which is required for activation of secretory copper enzymes including lysyl oxidase (LOX) and SOD3. This chaperone function is essential for full SOD3 and LOX enzymatic activity. Acts as a copper-dependent transcription factor. Upon copper binding, translocates to the nucleus where it binds specific promoter elements and regulates transcription of genes involved in cell proliferation, oxidative stress defense, and extracellular matrix remodeling. Activates expression of target genes including CCND1, SOD3 and NCF1, thereby linking cellular copper status to gene expression programs controlling growth and redox homeostasis

Homodimer (PubMed:24837030). Interacts with ATP7B (PubMed:10966647). Interacts with ATP7A (PubMed:19453293, PubMed:21667063). Interacts (via dimer form) with SLC31A1 (via C-terminal domain); this interaction improves ATOX1 stability and controls intracellular Cu(I) levels (PubMed:24837030, PubMed:26745413)
Primarily cytoplasmic; translocates to the nucleus in a copper- and stimulus-dependent manner

The heavy-metal-associated domain (HMA) coordinates a Cu(+) ion via the cysteine residues within the CXXC motif. The transfer of Cu(+) ion from ATOX1 to ATP7A involves the formation of a three-coordinate Cu(+)-bridged heterodimer where the metal is shared between the two metal binding sites of ATOX1 and ATP7A. The Cu(+) ion appears to switch between two coordination modes, forming two links with one protein and one with the other. Cisplatin, a chemotherapeutic drug, can bind the CXXC motif and hinder the release of Cu(+) ion
